brief: Build a brand identity direction for a new DTC skincare line called Cypress & Salt. Daily-use products, sourced botanicals, $40-70 price band. The brand wants to feel slow-craft and apothecary, not wellness-startup.

ideas.content: Identity built around a 19th-century pharmacy archive feel — heavy serif wordmark with discreet ligatures, deep umber labels on amber glass, batch numbers hand-stamped in cardinal red ink. Every product reads like it was bottled this morning in a small cellar.

Hand-drawn botanical illustrations (cypress, sea fennel, yarrow) rendered as scientific plates, each labeled with Latin binomial in fine italic. Wordmark in a humanist serif, cream paper, sage-green ink only. Reads as a herbarium of working ingredients.

Spare modernist system — wide-letterspaced sans-serif wordmark, all lowercase, in graphite on bone-white. Single accent stripe of pale coral runs across every label. Photography shot overhead on raw linen, daylight only. Cool and quiet.

Letterpressed kraft labels with a single embossed wave glyph. Wordmark in a wide all-caps grotesque. Palette pulled from kelp and seafoam. Letterpress impression deep enough to feel through the paper. Reads as analogue, durable, made-by-hand.

Unfinished brown chipboard labels with the wordmark Risograph-printed in two colours (deep blue and a single fluorescent orange). All product copy left ragged, no justification. Reads as architecture journal, not skincare.

Every product ships with a hand-tied jute twine carrying a small wooden tag burned with the wordmark. No printed labels at all — the tag IS the label. Glass bottles are unmarked. Maximum tactility. Costly to scale; the friction is the message.

Wordmark set in a custom-drawn serif with very low contrast, intentionally undynamic. Labels are bone-white paper, ink-black type, single line of italic Latin botanical name. No icons, no marks, no flourish. The restraint is the identity.

Brand surfaces are deep-black with the wordmark reversed-out in cream, set in a wide modern serif. Photography is high-key black-and-white film grain. Every touchpoint feels like a documentary monograph. Pairs with a typewriter monospace for support copy.

Backgrounds are continuous watercolour washes (sage, ochre, oxblood), with the wordmark hand-lettered in a calligraphic italic over each. Each batch has a slightly different colour wash so labels are subtly individual. Reads as artisan, intentionally imperfect.

Every product surface uses a stencil-print typography (chunky, vaguely military, broken edges) as if it were shipped overseas in a wooden crate. Palette: army green, manila, deep crimson. Reads as utilitarian, rationed, considered.

Identity built around a 12-column architectural grid. Wordmark sits inside the grid as one column-wide cell. Photography is shot against greenhouse glass, soft natural shadow only. Palette: pale moss, pale terracotta, wet stone. Reads as quiet horticultural authority.

Brand world expressed primarily through an annually-published thread-bound paper journal documenting the year's harvests, formulators, and field notes. The product packaging takes its visual cues from the journal. The brand is the publication; the products are episodes.
